summary: Fire tower and ranger's cabin on Spruce Mountain in the Smokies are gone; a 2019 trip report found only foundation blocks.

facts.status_note: The tower is gone; a 2019 trip report found only foundation blocks.

access.note: Reached on foot by the Spruce Mountain Trail in Great Smoky Mountains National Park, per a 2019 trip report.

visit.trail_note: A 1.2-mile in-and-out trail off Balsam Mountain Road ends at Campsite 42. No tower remains to climb.

evidence.supports: The site is listed in Haywood County, in Great Smoky Mountains National Park.
evidence.quote: Haywood County - Great Smoky Mountains National Park

evidence.supports: The name comes from the red spruce that grow on the mountain.
evidence.quote: Spruce Mountain is named for the red spruce that inhabit the area.

evidence.supports: Four years after the park was created, a fire tower and ranger's cabin were built on the summit.
evidence.quote: Four years after Congress created the Park, a fire tower and ranger’s cabin was built atop Spruce Mountain

evidence.supports: Electricity was installed at the same time, so power was connected then.
The tower is gone; what remains are foundation blocks overgrown with blackberry brambles.
evidence.quote: The tower is gone now and the only remnants are foundation blocks covered in thickets of blackberry brambles.

evidence.supports: The Polls Gap Trail ran near Balsam Mountain Campground and crossed the Spruce Mountain Trail until it was closed in 2000.
evidence.quote: Until being decommissioned in 2000, the Polls Gap Trail ran from Polls Gap (near Balsam Mountain Campground) and intersected Spruce Mountain Trail.

evidence.supports: A 2019 trip report describes reaching the site on foot.
evidence.quote: The hike from Balsam Mt. road is not difficult and only gains 700 feet.

evidence.supports: The trail covers 1.2 miles in and out, from one-lane Balsam Mountain Road.
evidence.quote: It is a 1.2 mile, in-and-out hiking destination located off a one-lane Balsam Mountain Road.
Campsite #42 is the terminus of the trail.

evidence.supports: Campsite 42 is in a clearing at the base of Spruce Mountain.
evidence.quote: It is nestled in a sparse clearing at the base of Spruce Mountain.

notes_for_editor: Only one recent description of the site exists: a 2019 trip report. It cites a 1999 Great Smoky Mountains Natural History Association book, which was not checked. The state list gives the park as agency and no dates. The build year is not given, only 'four years after Congress created the park', so a park or NPS history would be needed before a year is published. The site's remains and the trail's current condition are unverified. The story now dates the on-foot access to the 2019 report rather than saying it is true today.
